messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

He is a 70-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his life in close contact with other people’s pain, first learning to steady his hands as a young dentist and later becoming known in his community as someone calm, precise, and hard to rattle. That self-understanding changed the day of the bombing.

He remembers the morning with unusual clarity: the ordinary sounds of the office, the low hum of the drill, the smell of antiseptic, the familiar rhythm of patients coming and going. Terrorism had always seemed like something that happened elsewhere, in newspapers or on television, until it arrived in the form of a blast that shattered the building and the sense that the world obeys any rules at all. In the moment before impact, he is focused on a simple task at the chairside. In the moment after, he is on the floor, ears ringing, mouth full of dust, unable to make sense of the cries around him. Glass is everywhere. The room that had been carefully ordered minutes before is broken into fragments. He searches for colleagues and patients with a kind of stunned professionalism, as if his training might still matter in a place that has become unrecognizable.

In the days that follow, he functions because there is no other choice. He helps identify the injured, answers questions, fills out forms, calls family members, and returns to work as soon as he can tolerate being inside the building. Yet even then, he begins to notice that something in him remains at the site of the explosion. He startles at sudden noises, especially the sharp pop of balloons, construction bangs, or any unexpected metal sound. His body responds before his mind can catch up: his shoulders rise, his chest tightens, and for a moment he is back in the chaos of that day. He avoids the damaged side of town whenever possible and begins taking longer routes home. He no longer likes sitting with his back to a room, something he never used to think about.

As a dentist, he has always relied on fine motor control and concentration, but after the bombing he finds himself checking and rechecking simple steps. He worries about leaving instruments out, about locked doors, about whether he has heard the office alarm. He becomes more cautious with patients who come in agitated or loud, and he notices that he is less patient than he once was. At times, when he leans over a patient and the suction sounds too loud or the mask feels too tight, he has a brief sensation that he cannot breathe. He blinks, steadies himself, and carries on, though afterward he feels embarrassed by how much effort it takes to remain composed.

Night is harder than day. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly from dreams he cannot always remember in detail but that leave him drenched in sweat and disoriented, with the feeling that the bombing is happening again. He lies awake listening to the house settle, scanning the dark for danger. Since the death of his wife several years earlier, the silence at home has been difficult in a different way; after the attack, it becomes almost unbearable. She had been his main witness and source of comfort, the person who would have understood his need to talk through every detail. Without her, he keeps much of it inside. He speaks politely to his adult children and says he is “fine,” though they notice he is more withdrawn and less willing to join family gatherings, especially if they are held in crowded places.

He continues working because retirement feels too empty, and because the office gives him structure. Still, he senses that the event has narrowed his world. He is less likely to accept invitations, less likely to travel, and more likely to sit with old news in the background just for company, even if reports of attacks or violence make him tense. He remains proud of his competence, but he also knows that his confidence is no longer effortless. The bombing has made him alert in ways that never fully turn off, as if some part of him is always listening for the next explosion.
